title: Rav Ukva of Mishan
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: Shabbat 36b mentions him telling Rav Ashi, “You who are close to Rav and Shmuel,” etc. At 43a,
he said to Rav Ashi, “This works for the summer months,” etc.
Hyman reports that the Rosh, at the supplied locator לג:, says the ruling follows Rav Ashi because he is the later authority.
Hyman says that apparently he too took part with Rav Ashi in arranging the Talmud.

notes.text: The Rosh reference is printed לג:; whether this denotes a section or a folio in the intended printing remains unresolved. Hyman’s conjecture about arranging the Talmud is retained as a conjecture. The quoted sentence remains to be located at the supplied36b reference.

The Rosh's supplied לג: is restored literally; its function as section or edition-specific pagination is unresolved, and the former automatic 33b rendering is withdrawn. The earlier finite unsuccessful quotation search does not prove universal absence. Shabbat 36b and 43a remain Hyman's locators, with the latter introduction connected across units to Ukva's summer-months challenge to Rav Ashi. Hyman's APPARENTLY participation in arranging the Talmud remains his historical conjecture, not an established compiler role. Full Rav titles are supplied and preserved.

The consulted scan of Hyman, volume III, printed p. 979, has שבת לו: and the Rosh locator לג:, as in the supplied text. The directly consulted Rav Ukva–Rav Ashi exchange is at Shabbat 37b, not the supplied 36b; Davidson explains their closeness in terms of the place of Rav and Shmuel. The summer-months question begins at 43a and continues into 43b. The consulted Vilna-labeled digital Rosh on Shabbat 3:1:2 quotes the exchange and says that Rav Ashi, as the later authority, accepted Mar Ukva’s words in a discussion supporting Rabbi Yochanan’s ruling. Hyman’s description of this as ruling in accordance with Rav Ashi is retained as his report, without claiming identical wording or an established mapping of לג: to this digital address. His APPARENTLY taking part in arranging the Talmud remains his historical conjecture.
